corpus_definition: The system of trade and industry within a country.

forms.definition: the system of trade, industry and money in a country
forms.example: Tourism is important for the economy of Uzbekistan.

syn.note: The market is where buying and selling happen; the economy is the whole system.
Finance is about managing money, for a person, company or country.

forms.definition: to save money by spending less
forms.example: We had to economize on food after I lost my job.
forms.note: Belongs to economy = being careful with money (like economical), not a country's economy. British spelling: economise.

forms.definition: connected with trade, industry and money
forms.example: The country has had strong economic growth this year.
forms.note: Don't confuse with economical, which means 'not using much money or fuel'.

syn.note: Related: about money for a person or company too; economic is about a whole country.

forms.definition: not using much money, fuel or time
forms.example: This small car is very economical.
forms.note: Belongs to economy = being careful with money, not a country's economy. Don't confuse with economic.

forms.definition: in a way that is connected with trade, industry and money

syn.note: Related: in a way connected with money.

context.text: The government wants to grow the economy by building new factories. Experts say economic growth will be fastest in the cities, which are already doing well economically.

reviewer_note: Sense trap: economic (about the economy) vs economical (saving money). Map keeps only the 'system' sense.

people.definition: an expert who studies how money, trade and industry work
people.example: The economist said prices will rise next year.

people.definition: the subject that studies money, trade and industry
people.example: She is studying economics at university in Tashkent.

corpus_definition: To get something that is given or provided.

forms.definition: a piece of paper that shows you have paid for something
forms.example: Keep the receipt in case you want to return the shoes.
forms.note: The p is silent: /rɪˈsiːt/. In formal English it also means the act of receiving: 'on receipt of your letter'.

syn.note: Formal phrase used in shops and online.
Related, but careful: you get a bill BEFORE you pay and a receipt AFTER.

forms.definition: to get something that someone gives or sends you

syn.note: Everyday English; receive is more formal.
Formal: get something, often with effort.
Related: you agree to take it; you can receive something and not accept it.

ant.note: One person sends, the other receives.
One person gives, the other receives.

forms.definition: willing to listen to and accept new ideas
forms.example: The students were very receptive to the new teaching method.
forms.note: Belongs to receive = accept ideas or people, not getting a parcel. Same family: receive, reception, receptive.

forms.definition: in a way that shows you are willing to accept new ideas
forms.example: She listened receptively to every suggestion.
forms.note: Goes with receptive. Very rare; most people say 'with an open mind'.

context.text: I received a parcel from my aunt today. Inside there was a book and a receipt, so I can change it if I already have it.

reviewer_note: False-prefix trap: 're-' + 'ceive' is not a real split; no affix is claimed.

people.definition: the part of a phone or radio that gets the signal
people.example: He picked up the receiver and said hello.

people.definition: a person who gets something, such as a prize or letter
people.example: The recipient of the award was a young teacher.

people.definition: a person who welcomes visitors at a hotel or office
people.example: The receptionist gave us the room key.
people.note: Belongs to receive = welcome guests (reception), not getting a parcel.

corpus_definition: Stop doing something that you used to do regularly.
particle_note: Separable: 'give up sugar' or 'give sugar up'. Often followed by -ing: 'give up smoking'.

relations.note: Very close and a little informal, common in American English: "quit smoking".
Stop is general; give up suggests a habit you had for a long time.
To start a new hobby or habit: "She took up yoga."

context.text: My uncle gave up smoking three years ago. He says it was hard, but giving up was the best decision of his life.

corpus_definition: To check that something is true or has been done.
usage_note: make sure + (that) + clause: 'Make sure (that) the door is locked.' Also make sure + to do: 'Make sure to call me.'

relations.note: Check is about looking; make sure is about being certain that something is done.
More formal, common in writing: 'Please ensure the form is signed.'

context.text: Before we leave for Samarkand, make sure you have your passport. I always make sure the windows are closed too.
